---
title: "P1 exercise — Explain the structure"
---

Work from the [tutorial](index.qmd). Allow about 45–60 minutes, including
discussion. These classroom descriptions are invented; they are not substitute
microscope images or instructions for handling specimens. Leave with labelled
drawings and short mechanistic explanations. No software is needed.

## 1. Follow material through a leaf

Draw epidermis, a stomatal pore, an internal air space, mesophyll, xylem and
phloem. Trace CO2, water and exported carbohydrate using separate labelled
arrows. Mark where at least one membrane must be crossed. Explain why opening
the pore can increase both carbon access and water loss. Do not draw phloem as
an extension of the stomatal pore.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Start with compartments

CO2 reaches mesophyll from the atmosphere; water arrives through vascular
tissue. A photosynthetic product's eventual export is a different pathway.
An arrow between organs is not a claim that no membranes lie along the route.
:::

## 2. Classify evidence, not just names

For each invented observation, identify a plausible cell/tissue function and
one additional feature needed before a confident identification.

| Description | Observation |
| --- | --- |
| A | An elongated conducting element lacks living contents and has thick lignified walls |
| B | A living photosynthetic cell borders a large internal air space |
| C | A living epidermal cell has a long extension into the surrounding soil |
| D | A population near a shoot tip contains small actively dividing cells |

Why would “thick wall” alone fail to identify xylem? Why does a text exercise
not demonstrate that you can recognise the tissue on an actual slide?

## 3. Root growth has more than one explanation

In this invented simplified model, a marked root segment contains 100 cells
arranged end to end. Ignore gaps and assume the measured cell length represents
the whole segment. Mean length is 40 µm before and 70 µm after a period with
no divisions. Calculate segment length at both times in millimetres and its
increase. Compare with a second case containing 175 cells of 40 µm each.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check the scale

100 × 40 µm = 4000 µm = 4 mm; 100 × 70 µm = 7 mm. The increase is 3 mm.
175 × 40 µm is also 7 mm. Equal final lengths can arise through different
cellular processes. Real tissue has heterogeneous cell lengths and geometry.
:::

## 4. Pressure is not the entire growth mechanism

A cell rapidly takes up water but does not undergo irreversible expansion.
Offer two compatible explanations involving the wall or growth state. What
observation would distinguish temporary swelling from lasting growth? Explain
why wall loosening and synthesis must be coordinated.

## 5. Three genomes, one cell

An invented mutation changes a nuclear gene encoding a protein imported into
chloroplasts. The chloroplast DNA sequence is unchanged, but photosynthetic
performance decreases. Is this contradictory? Explain protein location versus
gene location. Then explain how two tissues sharing a nuclear genome can have
different organelles and functions without invoking different DNA sequences.

## Completion check

Your answers should distinguish tissues from organs, membranes from walls,
division from expansion and gene location from protein destination. Return to
the [self-check](quiz.qmd) after revising one explanation from discussion.
